c.st: Fully Functional 1KB Hard Drive in Vanilla Minecraft
c.x:
Besides "Code," I highly recommend "The Pattern on the Stone" by Danny Hillis, who also happens to be the designer of Thinking Machines' massively parallel supercomputer, the Connection Machine. It covers more material than Code in a lot less time.

In "Code," Petzold makes sure to cover the material exteremely slowly so that you won't miss any details, so it may get boring for some, but I would also read Code if you have the time and interest.

c.st: Ask HN: What are the most eye-opening textbooks you have ever read?
c.x:
Code, by Petzold.

Not exactly eye-opening, I sort of knew most of the content, but I don't remember ever having such joy while reading a technical book. Before or since.

I read the whole thing in a holiday (it's a big book, 500 pages or more IIRC), and I am a terrible reader. I was at a place with no internet, so that surely helped a lot.

Not necessarily gamify but make it fun. I recommend 'Code' by Petzold. This book explains how computers work and has some methoids how to add numbers or build an adder yourself and it is super fun to read.

c.st: Ask HN: What's the "best" book you've ever read?
c.x:
"The Death and Life of Great American Cities" by Jane Jacobs.

This book completely changed how I view my city and other urban areas. I am now much more in-tune with my urban environment and understand how different aspects of it affect me emotionally.

It also led me to going back to graduate school for a degree in urban design and sustainability, and my focus is now how I can use my computer science background to improve my environment.

c.st: The Decline of the City Grid
c.x:
Tucked away in the middle of any urban planning article is a reference to Jane Jacob's "The Death and Life of Great American Cities". It's a great book that puts into words why certain neighborhoods cities feel alive and fit for humans. From mixed-use buildings to small blocks to sidewalks to parks to landmarks.

I'm not going to say her insights are universal for everyone, but it might help you understand why you like that grid you like.

This is completely false. Read her classic, "The Death and Life of Great American Cities." She's trying to get at what makes cities work (variety and density). IIRC she talks about 100 units per acre as the right balance. This is what that looks like:

https://www.theurbanist.org/2017/05/04/visualizing-compatible-density/

But yes, she was against destroying neighborhoods with freeways.

c.st: Ask HN: As a person, what can I do to improve a city?
c.x:
I'd recommend reading some of Jane Jacob's work, specifically 
The Death and Life of Great American Cities. It illustrates the ideas of street life and what makes great places.

As for a direct idea, I'd try to get to know your neighbours, walk in your neighbourhood as often as possible, and support your local businesses.

hn.q: "The Death and Life of Great American Cities"
